entries.title: The Court’s Ballroom Decision Is a Sign of Deeper Problems
entries.summary: The conservative justices have separation of powers exactly backwards.
entries.content:
The conservative justices have separation of powers exactly backwards.

In deciding to allow President Trump to proceed with constructing a new ballroom, which Congress has not authorized, at the White House, which Trump does not own, the U.S. Supreme Court invoked the separation of powers. But the Court got the constitutional problem precisely backwards: The separation-of-powers problem isn’t that courts are impermissibly blocking the president’s use of taxpayer funds to create a ballroom. It’s that the president is impermissibly using unauthorized taxpayer funds to create a ballroom.

The Court’s missteps were many, starting in the very first sentence of its opinion: “In October 2025, the federal government started a project to replace the East Wing of the White House.” (The opinion, decided via the Court’s shadow docket, was per curiam, meaning that it did not indicate an author, but because the four dissenters noted their names, we know the five justices in the majority were Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.)

But the federal government didn’t begin replacing part of the White House. Only the president and the executive branch did. Under the U.S. Constitution, the president is not the be-all and end-all of the federal government. Far from it: The legislature, Congress, is the body that has the power to establish and regulate federal property (including the White House) and to authorize the spending of federal funds. Indeed, the plaintiff in the case—the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States—argued that the president was proceeding without congressional authorization and in violation of federal laws. The Supreme Court majority did not say otherwise, making no claim as to whether the ballroom-construction project was legal or whether the president had the authority to undertake it.

The Supreme Court’s conflation of the president with the federal government is the latest iteration in the Court’s steady embrace of the unitary-executive theory and the accompanying expansion of executive power. This theory maintains that all executive power resides in the president, and that Congress cannot limit the president’s exercise of that power. Yet these days, the president, occasionally with the Court’s blessing, is claiming to possess legislative powers too. That is the case when the president declines to spend funds that Congress has obligated or when the president decides to spend funds that Congress has not authorized. Under the Constitution, Congress, not the president, has the power of the purse. Nevertheless, the unitary-executive theory unites all government power in the president, paving the way for an executive unbound by law.

The Court’s errors continued as justices attempted to explain why the lower courts were wrong to block the president’s demolition of a portion of the White House. The Court relied on the doctrine of standing, which maintains that a plaintiff challenging the government’s actions must show that they have been injured by the actions they are contesting. In this case, one of the members of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who lives in Washington, D.C., and about once a month visits the neighborhood where the White House is located, alleged that she had “aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests” in what happened there.

Under the Court’s precedents, that injury should have sufficed. Indeed, in a prior opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, the Court had said that desire to “observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes,” can constitute “a cognizable interest for purpose of standing.” Crocodiles and all animals are great and important, to be sure. But so is the White House. As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his dissent, “The White House is not just any building.” It is “an iconic American building whose symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture.”

The doctrine of standing, the Court has said, is a vital component of the separation of powers, because it ensures that the judicial branch stays within its role rather than encroaching on the other branches, specifically the executive. But in this case, as in others, the Court has invoked the doctrine to support the flow of power in one direction only: limiting Congress’s authority while expanding the president’s. In the ballroom case, the Court said the National Trust member did not have standing to sue, and therefore the plaintiff (and the federal courts) could not enforce the federal statutes that the president was allegedly violating. Following the decision, it’s unclear who, if anyone, can sue to enforce the federal laws that the plaintiffs allege the president is violating with the ballroom-construction project.

That is the effect of many of the Court’s standing cases—to render congressional statutes unenforceable. In TransUnion v. Ramirez, the Court said that a group of plaintiffs who were incorrectly designated as suspected drug traffickers and terrorists in their credit reports could not sue to enforce Fair Credit Reporting Act provisions requiring consumer-reporting agencies to maintain accurate records. As a result of that decision, the FCRA provisions go largely unenforced. In Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife and Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation, the Court said that plaintiffs seeking to enforce the Endangered Species Act and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, among other laws, did not have standing, and thus could not enforce those laws either. Far from ensuring the separation of powers, the Court has used standing to undermine the principle: According to the Constitution, Congress has the power to make laws, but the Court’s standing decisions have freed the executive branch (and other entities) from having to comply with them.

The Court made its final error in its analysis of the relevant harms in the case. To obtain emergency relief on the shadow docket, the party seeking relief (here, the president, as he was appealing the lower court’s injunction) is supposed to show that they would suffer irreparable harm if the Court does not act. The Court said the president is irreparably harmed because the lower court overstepped its powers, and undermined the separation of powers, by blocking the president’s actions. But if the president’s actions are illegal, it is more than a little odd to say that stopping them injures the president. That would essentially mean that at least some limits on the president’s power are unenforceable, because enforcing them would injure the president.

This is not the first decision to raise that harrowing implication. In a 2025 nationwide injunction case related to the birthright-citizenship executive order, the Court said the president was irreparably harmed because the lower courts had blocked an executive order—later determined to be unconstitutional—on a nationwide basis. Similarly, in the recent mail-in-ballot decision, the Court said the president was irreparably harmed because lower courts had blocked an executive order—one that is likely illegal—too soon, and before the plaintiffs experienced an injury.

It is fine and good to ensure that lower courts are acting within the bounds of their authority. But the separation of powers demands that the Supreme Court stop undermining Congress’s power to make meaningful laws by allowing the executive to violate them without consequence.

entries.title: The White House Wants to Make the Smithsonian a Pariah
entries.summary: A renewed threat underscores the museum complex’s isolation—and the limits of Trump’s pressure campaign.
entries.content:
A renewed threat underscores the museum complex’s isolation—and the limits of Trump’s pressure campaign.

The Trump administration’s latest strategy to control the Smithsonian has the logic of lunchroom bullying; the Department of Interior is channeling “you can’t sit with us” energy as it tries to make the world’s largest museum complex a pariah in Washington.

In a newly public August 28 letter from the department to the Smithsonian board of regents, Trump-administration officials write that executive departments and agencies “cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership” and suggest that they cease cooperation with the Smithsonian on routine logistical matters, such as loaning items for exhibits and awarding discretionary grants. The letter was sent just days before the regents, having failed to secure an open site on the National Mall for the Smithsonian’s newest museums, resorted to placing the National Museum of the American Latino in a largely vacant building it already owns. In doing so, the Smithsonian dodged Congress, a move that reflects the inward turn of an institution on the outs.

Such developments illustrate the growing alienation the Smithsonian faces in the capital and difficulties that go deeper than the superficial signage Donald Trump wants placed in front of one of its museums to discredit it. For the past year and a half, the White House has repeatedly threatened the institution, but recently, more parties have joined the effort—first Republicans in Congress who in two hearings scrutinized the National Museum of American History over supposed partisan bias, and now the Interior Department, which has no official oversight of the Smithsonian. Although partially government-funded, the Smithsonian is independent of the executive branch—the White House has essentially no say over what it does—and it was designed to be as such. Still, it’s becoming clear that functioning freely in this charged climate might also mean going it alone.

Invoking the White House’s recent report on the Museum of American History, the Interior letter accuses the Smithsonian of potentially violating federal antidiscrimination laws—a common way, on the right, of criticizing DEI programs, especially those created in response to the racial-justice protests of the late 2010s and early 2020s. Signed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy Vince Haley, the letter also requests a meeting with the board of regents, the entity that actually oversees the institution. The regents’ membership has been shrinking this year as members’ terms have ended and their positions have gone unfilled, reportedly due to administration pressure.

Despite the language in the letter, a White House official told me by email that the Interior Department did not mean that agencies shouldn’t cooperate with the Smithsonian; rather, those agencies will “find it difficult to cooperate with current Smithsonian leadership in light of the disturbing evidence that has been uncovered.” The official also said it’s up to the Justice Department to determine whether the Smithsonian violated antidiscrimination laws and not to conflate “evidence of unlawful discrimination with a direct allegation that it happened.”

In the letter, the Interior Department writes that institution leadership has embraced “radical ideology” that serves to “weaken our shared American identity” and “erase our heritage.” The rhetoric is particularly striking coming from the department at the center of contested efforts to take down wall texts at National Park sites across the country, where information on slavery, climate change, Native Americans, and other topics has been removed over the past year. The National Park Service represents a discomfiting alternate reality for the Smithsonian—one in which exhibits have been subject to political approval.

The White House is surely pleased with such changes at the National Park sites, which Trump called for in the same March 2025 executive order that kicked off the administration’s campaign against the Smithsonian. It seems to want to extend that kind of control to the museums on the National Mall, which Trump has asserted are too negative and focus too much on “how bad slavery was.” But with a president-proof system standing in officials’ way, they’ve had to seek out additional levers of pressure against Smithsonian leadership.

The Interior letter represents the department’s most comprehensive public statement on the Smithsonian after the White House tapped it in July to place signs on National Park Service–controlled land outside the National Museum of American History, which will detail its alleged political biases and direct would-be visitors to what the administration describes as more accurate information. Much of this effort is about framing U.S. history in a more positive light, which the Smithsonian says it already does while also dealing with that history’s complexities.

These partisan feuds are especially familiar to the Museum of the American Latino, which was subject to politicized scrutiny long before Trump started taking on the wider institution. Foreshadowing present criticisms, a 2022 Heritage Foundation op-ed described one of the museum’s early shows as a disgrace with an “unabashedly Marxist portrayal of history, religion and economics.” Writers for the right-wing think tank asserted that the museum should be defunded, a call one of them repeated this summer (and he threw in the Women’s History Museum for good measure).

The Museum of the American Latino’s placement in the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building will surely disappoint some: No starchitect to deliver a glossy new design. No bespoke architecture, like the Museum of the American Indian’s sinuous facade or the Museum of African American History and Culture’s Yoruba-crown-inspired exterior. It might make for a quieter debut. Then again, the World’s Fair–style building is arguably the loudest, most colorful structure on the National Mall. It certainly won’t look like a museum that anyone is trying to hide.

entries.title: The Truth About American Food Safety
entries.summary: Have sprawling outbreaks become the norm?
entries.content:
The phrase When it rains, it pours isn’t one you like to see applied to outbreaks of foodborne illness, yet here we are. The summer started with a diarrhea-causing parasite called Cyclospora cayetanensis, which infested iceberg lettuce. Then came news of Shiga toxin–producing bacteria in organic frozen berries, and a Salmonella outbreak linked to Whole Foods guacamole that eventually got traced to tainted jalapeños. (Pico de gallo, salsa fresca, and a variety of spicy dips have also been implicated.) Ricotta-style cheese was recalled for Listeria. Both Salmonella and E. coli were found in products from the aptly named Everything Sprouts. And 10,000 cases of lightly fried tofu were flagged for potential contamination with printing ink.

This flood of food-contamination events comes at just the time when our systems to prevent such outbreaks may be hobbled. Since last year, three cyclospora-research projects at the Department of Agriculture have lost either their funding or staffing, the CDC team that tracks the parasite’s genetics has nearly disappeared, and experienced government employees responsible for food safety have left their job or been fired.

The bureaucracy is crumbling, and the produce aisle is a mess. But let’s be fair: The status quo on foodborne illness was never very good. According to 2019 estimates from the CDC, Americans suffer (sometimes unaware) through at least 9.9 million bouts of foodborne illness each year; more than 50,000 people end up in the hospital, and about 1,000 die. Depending on how you measure outbreak numbers—whether by FDA investigations into foodborne illnesses, for instance, or by the number of food-product recalls—the 2026 statistics have been pretty much in line with recent history. How quickly we forget the Salmonella-dusted cucumbers of summer 2024 that sickened more than 500 souls. Or the cantaloupes that killed half a dozen people in 2023. Occasional salad-based catastrophes have been the norm for many years. Food-safety experts say that something on the order of 150 million meals of leafy greens are served in this country every day. Now as always, a very small proportion of them will make you ill.

But one of this summer’s outbreaks does suggest that our “very small proportion” might be growing into a slightly larger very small proportion. Although the jalapeño and berry outbreaks have had many doleful precedents of their size and scope, the cyclospora summer stands alone. Annual cases of its associated diarrheal disease, called cyclosporiasis, have been slowly increasing over time, from hundreds in the 2010s to a few thousand in the early 2020s. (This is, in part, due to faster diagnosis: One used to have to find the parasite’s oocysts under a microscope; now the fragments of its DNA can be identified in a rapid-PCR screening test.) This year, though, the CDC has confirmed 17,180 cases of the illness, and many thousands more suspected cases still need to be examined. State-level agencies have tallied more than 30,000 infections. “It’s just absolutely crazy,” Kalmia Kniel, an expert in microbial food safety at the University of Delaware and a former president of the International Association for Food Protection, told me. “It is completely overwhelming and insane that this happened.” I suppose it’s nice to know the sense of overwhelm afflicts experts too.

No one seems to know exactly how or why this year’s cyclosporiasis caseload got so big. The largest group of cases, which has been centered in the upper Midwest, has been linked to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico. Kniel suspects that in Michigan, the parasite may have worked its way from the feces of the first infected people into the local water supply, spawning a secondary, local outbreak. Michael Osterholm, who runs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy and previously spent 15 years as the state’s head epidemiologist, told me that he’s seen no evidence to support the secondary-outbreak theory. Either way, some mystery remains as to how the parasite got into the food supply in Mexico. Taylor Farms, which recalled its iceberg lettuce in July, is “one of the leading produce companies in terms of food safety,” Kniel said. And yet here we are.

Perhaps the government could be doing more to resolve some of this uncertainty. On this point, though, expert opinions vary widely. Kniel said that, at least at first, the FDA and the CDC appeared to be posting information about the cyclospora situation more slowly than they had in past years. Steven Mandernach, the executive director of the Association of Food and Drug Officials and a former food-safety official in Iowa, told me that as far as he can tell, information has been coming out just as efficiently as ever. Osterholm believes that the sky is falling. “We have hit an all-time low, in my 50 years in public health, in our capacity to identify and respond to foodborne outbreaks,” he said, adding that the government’s slow response time on the cyclospora outbreak was nothing less than “public-health malpractice.” In an emailed statement, Grace Davis Jamison, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson, wrote, “Claims that HHS has lacked transparency overlook the extensive information FDA and CDC have shared as investigations progress including timely updates that help the public understand potential risks and make informed decisions.” She also said that no FDA investigators had been lost to staffing changes, and that the CDC laboratory that supports foodborne-outbreak investigations was likewise “unaffected.”

Perhaps this disagreement can be squared by acknowledging the failings of the past. The system has long been underfunded while needed changes were delayed, Barbara Kowalcyk, the director of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security, told me. The recent departures of experienced personnel, to retirements and layoffs, have made things only worse. “We had one hand tied behind our back before this administration happened, and now we have both hands tied,” she said. (How exactly this might translate into disease outbreaks in years ahead remains unclear.)

History suggests that few new investments in food safety come before a tragic outbreak of disease. “It was the 1993 Jack in the Box outbreak that really changed things at USDA,” Kowalcyk said, referring to the undercooked, contaminated hamburgers that killed four children who had eaten at the fast-food chain. A 2006 outbreak of E. coli in bagged spinach, which caused hundreds of illnesses and $200 million in lost spinach sales, helped inspire the passage of the Food Safety Modernization Act. Now we have the cyclospora summer. “I think that this is going to drive another paradigm shift,” Kowalcyk said.

Cyclosporiasis is, by the grace of God, a relatively gentle and self-limiting disease. Many people recover on their own within a few weeks. And for all of the tens of thousands of cases that have been registered in recent months (and the many more infections that were never diagnosed), just two deaths have been reported. Their loss is a tragedy; the economic devastation caused by falling lettuce prices, and the fact that many consumers have spent months in fear of eating leafy greens, is a shame. But given that this summer’s cyclospora plague stands among the largest foodborne-illness outbreaks in the nation’s history, these outcomes seem modest.

Consider this a solace and a warning: Our summer of contamination could have been much worse.

entries.title: The Air Marshals Keeping Watch On Eric Swalwell
entries.summary: The FBI made a highly irregular request to monitor one of Trump’s most visible critics.
entries.content:
The FBI made a highly irregular request to monitor one of Trump’s most visible critics.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

On August 8, former Representative Eric Swalwell boarded a United Airlines flight from Frankfurt, Germany, to Washington, D.C. He didn’t know it, but federal agents were watching him throughout the nine-hour trip.

The FBI had asked the Federal Air Marshal Service to covertly monitor Swalwell on board and to watch him use his electronic devices, to see whether its officers could visually ascertain his passcodes, according to records I obtained that have not previously been reported on. Air marshals are trained to blend in with other passengers and quietly keep tabs on their subjects, who are usually suspected terrorists or potential hijackers, not politicians.

But Swalwell is an enemy of sorts to the Trump administration. For years, the Democrat has been one of Donald Trump’s most visible political antagonists, having served as a manager in the president’s second impeachment trial. Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller has called Swalwell a “scumbag” on national television. And FBI Director Kash Patel, the leader of the agency that wanted Swalwell monitored, described him as one of the “corrupt actors of the first order” in his 2023 book, Government Gangsters.

The directive for air-marshal surveillance said that Swalwell was the “focus” of an FBI investigation, but it didn’t provide additional details. Law enforcement has good reason to investigate the 45-year-old. This past spring, a former staff member accused Swalwell of twice raping her while she was intoxicated. A woman in California accused Swalwell of drugging and raping her after he’d promised to assist with her career. Three more women have accused Swalwell of making unwanted advances and sending them lewd text messages, including nude pictures of himself. Swalwell has denied the allegations, but authorities in Los Angeles and Manhattan have opened a criminal investigation. In April, as the number of accusers mounted, Swalwell suspended his campaign for governor of California and resigned from his seat in Congress.

A week after the flight from Germany, Swalwell got off another plane at San Francisco International Airport. FBI agents were waiting for him with a search warrant. They seized his mobile phone and personal computer. (It’s not clear whether, by that point, the FBI knew the passcodes to unlock those devices.) The next day, agents searched Swalwell’s home in Washington, D.C. Documents filed in federal court in California suggest that the bureau is investigating Swalwell in connection with the sexual-assault cases in Los Angeles and New York.

Despite the seriousness of the accusations against Swalwell, many aspects of the FBI’s request to the Federal Air Marshal Service were unusual, current and former officials told me. For one thing, the FBI does not usually investigate sexual assault. For another, asking air marshals to obtain a subject’s electronic passcodes is considered out of the ordinary even for traditional subjects of surveillance, one former official said. The agency presumes that requests for assistance from the FBI, which are not unusual, are relevant to a legitimate investigation. But the bureau’s behavior here undermines that confidence, the former official added.

The request to monitor Swalwell was classified as “Special Mission Coverage,” a term for ad hoc requests from law-enforcement or intelligence agencies that don’t involve people on security watch lists. The FBI’s decision to ask air marshals for help also puzzled some former law-enforcement officials I spoke with, who asked why the FBI hadn’t put its own agents on the plane to conduct surveillance, which would have been a routine matter.

Given the public evidence and the history of the Trump administration’s efforts to investigate or discredit Swalwell, current and former officials and security experts told me that they have trouble imagining that the federal government would have gone to such lengths if the accused were not one of the administration’s least favorite people. They spoke on the condition of anonymity because they didn’t want to provoke reprisals.

Sara Azari, Swalwell’s lawyer, told me in a statement that Swalwell has been in contact with the Department of Justice throughout the assault investigation. “Not once were we asked for Mr. Swalwell’s phones or devices. Had the DOJ asked, we would have complied, as we have with every other request,” she said. Azari called the air-marshal surveillance an “extraordinary escalation” against her client, who has not been charged with a crime.

The FBI declined to comment. The Transportation Security Administration, which runs the air-marshals service, didn’t respond to emails and phone calls requesting comment.

The midair surveillance of the former lawmaker is not the only unusual step the federal government has taken in this case. The warrant used to seize Swalwell’s electronic devices cited a civil-rights statute that historically has been applied to police officers who abuse their authority while acting “under color of law.” It traces its origins to the 19th century and was used in the 1960s to charge local police in Mississippi who conspired with Klansmen to murder civil-rights workers. Decades later, two of the police officers who’d beaten Rodney King were convicted under the law. And it was used to bring federal charges against Derek Chauvin, the officer convicted in Minnesota of killing George Floyd.

The FBI hasn’t publicly articulated its rationale for applying the law to Swalwell. But one theory, according to legal experts I spoke with, may be that he used the power of his office to intimidate his alleged victims into silence. Prosecutors might believe that there’s evidence of coercion or threats in Swalwell’s electronic communications.

But it’s not clear that the law would apply to a legislator as it does to law-enforcement officials, who have the power to detain people. “Mr. Swalwell’s private relationships between consenting adults have nothing to do with his office, his authority, or his official duties,” his lawyer said.

The fact that details about the search of Swalwell’s devices and home are publicly known is also a departure from usual law-enforcement procedure. The inventory of what the agents took from him at the San Francisco airport, which should have been kept under seal, was somehow made public.

Under Patel, the FBI has publicized its investigative steps against high-profile suspects before they have been charged. In August 2025, Patel posted on X about an imminent FBI action just as agents began raiding the home of former National Security Adviser John Bolton, a Trump critic. Broadcasting a secret operation in advance could tip off a suspect and potentially put agents in physical danger. At least one news organization appeared to have known ahead of time about the Bolton raid. A month later, Patel posted that “the subject” in the murder of Charlie Kirk was in custody, hours before it was true. He also posted details about leads that agents were following in the Kirk case, which could have jeopardized the investigation.

It’s possible that the FBI is interested in Swalwell for reasons that go beyond his alleged treatment of women. The Department of Homeland Security is investigating his employment of a nanny from Brazil. Swalwell is also among the Trump critics whom Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte criminally referred to the Department of Justice over alleged mortgage fraud. Swalwell has never been charged, however, and experts have pointed out that Pulte’s allegations against officials probably reflect paperwork errors, not genuine attempts to defraud lenders.

Swalwell was also once a subject in a counterintelligence investigation of a suspected agent for China’s intelligence service. But in 2017, the FBI cleared him, and the Justice Department didn’t file charges. A former U.S. official familiar with the case told me that the representative had cooperated with investigators after they’d presented him with evidence that the woman he knew might be a foreign operative.

Last month, the administration made the unusual decision to publicly release classified FBI files related to that investigation. Swalwell’s conservative critics have long been obsessed with the case of Christine Fang, known as Fang Fang, who the files show was suspected of working for China’s Ministry of State Security. The files helped the public understand more details about Chinese espionage. But they also revealed that Swalwell had admitted to having a physical relationship with Fang. Embarrassing Swalwell might have been the point of disclosing the documents.

Patel has made no secret of his contempt for Swalwell. During a House Judiciary Committee hearing last September, when Swalwell was a member, they sparred over whether Trump’s name appeared in files from the investigation of Jeffrey Epstein, and what Patel had told then–Attorney General Pam Bondi about the matter. Swalwell accused Patel of being evasive and showing “consciousness of guilt.”

Swalwell then cited Patel’s book, in which Swalwell’s name appears on a list of “deep state” actors. Twenty of those people, Swalwell said, had already been investigated or faced “adverse actions.” He asked whether Patel would recuse himself from any investigations of the people he had named, including Swalwell.

“I’m going to borrow your terminology and call bullshit on your entire career in Congress. It has been a disgrace to the American people,” Patel said. The two men spoke over each other.

Finally, the FBI director answered Swalwell’s question. “No,” he said, he would not recuse.

Madison Hahamy and Marie-Rose Sheinerman contributed research to this story.

*Illustration Sources: Tierney L. Cross / Bloomberg / Getty; Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc / Getty.

entries.title: Inside a Conservative Operation to Hijack Your Social-Media Feed
entries.summary: A service run from Latvia offers payment for short, social-media-friendly clips designed to look like grassroots GOP support.
entries.content:
A service run from Latvia offers payment for short, social-media-friendly clips designed to look like grassroots GOP support.

If you’re short on cash, there is someone in Riga, Latvia, who can help. “You can literally make 100k a month with this campaign,” a young man with blond curls and a thick accent says into a camera. All you have to do is post on social media video clips of “anything that supports Republican.” Unfamiliar with U.S. politics? No problem: “If you’re not from the USA, like, What the fuck is even Republicans? like me,” then simply go to Gemini or ChatGPT, he suggests, “and be like ‘Yo, Gemini, I want some videos promoting Republican values. Give me ideas.’ Go to Gemini. Get ideas. Boom.”

The man, who goes by Serviuos, is promoting a campaign called Elephant Clipping, run by his company, ClipIt. The company pays subcontractors, many from poorer countries in Eastern Europe and the global South, to chop up videos the company provides into bite-size pieces in the hope that the clips will go viral online.

Such “clipping” operations have become a popular means of manipulating people’s attention. Brands, influencers, musical artists, and others spend six-figure sums on such promotional campaigns. Perhaps inevitably, the practice is now moving into politics, often without the transparency required to know exactly what is being served up and by whom. Five months before the midterms, though, Serviuos is up-front about the goal of the Elephant Clipping campaign: “So that republican win in USA,” he writes in one message. I sent Serviuos a list of questions about his work in American right-wing politics. He wrote back, “Seems very out of context,” but didn’t comment further.

Many video-clipping services operate in relative secrecy so that the public isn’t aware of the manipulation of their social-media feeds. But the services also need to attract potential clippers. They typically rely on chat servers on Discord—an internet messaging app that was initially developed for gamers.

After an anonymous tipster flagged Elephant Clipping to me, I was able to access its Discord server and other related political-clipping campaign chats just by clicking “Join,” noting on a form that I was based in the United States, and answering some questions about my availability and desire to clip. Once I was in, I could see the mechanics of the campaign, which pays huge sums of money to people—many of whom appeared to be outside the U.S.—to push video clips from accounts designed to look like those of ordinary Americans spontaneously touting reasons to favor the GOP.

In one channel on the server, users can submit pro-Republican videos that they’ve already posted on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts to be reviewed for payment. A separate Google Drive contains suggested videos for clippers to use, but “you can clip anything as long as it is positively framed conservative pro-Republican content,” Serviuos explains to participants. He provides some examples: a video of “Top 5 Joe Rogan moments,” a video of a conservative YouTuber confronting liberals with the suggested caption “See how Nick Shirley handles being told to ‘get the f* out’ of a public property.” Clippers are paid a proportionate share of the campaign’s monthly budget of $300,000. Every 1 million views yields a $300 payout.

The videos that result are not publicly visible in the Discord. Some clipper accounts on social media, however, inadvertently revealed their participation in the campaign by repeating the 258-word “Goal of the Campaign” instructions in the captions of some of their short videos. The Instagram account @_politicalhub, for example, posted the caption alongside a video of Charlie Kirk calling Palestine a “nonexistent place.” Another account called @frontrawpolitics posted the instructional text in the caption of a video of a conservative influencer saying that she would never marry a liberal, “because he’s going to raise my son to be a faggot.” Each video had only a single like, but both accounts had posted other videos, without the instructional caption, that collectively accrued tens of thousands of views.

The instructions contain no directive to add a disclosure that the video may result in the poster being paid or that it is part of an organized campaign. Clippers are instructed to use U.S.-based proxy servers and to hide their location on social media to obfuscate that they’re working from outside the United States. The server also doesn’t disclose who’s funding any of this. But it does leave some clues that lead to a relative of a Republican mega-donor.

Elephant Clipping’s operation is the newest version of “astroturfing”—orchestrated messaging designed to look like genuine expressions of grassroots support. In the 2016 election cycle, the Internet Research Agency, a Kremlin-linked troll farm outside St. Petersburg, tried to influence the U.S. presidential election with fake social-media posts, bot farms, and protests organized through Facebook. Teens in Macedonia also posted incendiary disinformation about U.S. politics in a bid to generate advertising revenue from the number of clicks they generated on Google and other platforms. Serviuos’s clipping operations—Elephant Clipping is just one of them—are driving views to the cause they are being paid to promote.

Isabel Linzer, a policy analyst at the Center for Democracy and Technology, a Washington, D.C.–based think tank, told me that the existence of political clip farms operating at scale, such as Elephant Clipping, had been suspected but hadn’t previously been confirmed. Earlier reports revealed more targeted operations. MS NOW, for instance, recently reported on a campaign in which influencers were paid to post videos supportive of the Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens. (She lost her primary race in Michigan last month anyway.) Linzer noted that Elephant Clipping stands out for the apparent scale of the investment and for its attempt to create faux grassroots support.

In the Discord server I accessed, one of Serviuos’s associates touts the campaign as “a once in a lifetime opportunity” to be a part of what “could be the biggest clipping campaign in the entire industry.” Hyperbole, perhaps. And comparisons are hard to come by, because many of these campaigns involve private chat rooms. But the numbers that Elephant Clipping claims are very large. The operation aims to hit 1 billion views a month on videos its clippers post. It often falls short of that goal, but the campaign still regularly accrues hundreds of millions of views a week, according to automated campaign updates, which could not be independently verified. Serviuos seems to have been running the campaign for some time: Discord records for Elephant Clipping’s budget go back only to April, but the campaign has been going on for “about a year now,” Serviuos said in a video posted that month.

My examination of Elephant Clipping led me to several other, similar clipping campaigns that appeared linked to Serviuos and that all appeared to be pushing conservative content. Another site visible on the server, Monster Lab, displays large clipping-campaign budgets that have now ended. One “political clipping” campaign that ran in February displays a $900,000 budget. Two other campaigns that ran in March and April, which involved making clips of a famous “U.S. political commentator,” also each listed a $900,000 monthly budget. Yet another campaign that ran last month had a $120,000 budget and instructed clippers to post videos edited from the YouTube channel of Turning Point USA, the conservative nonprofit organization co-founded by the late Charlie Kirk. It also links to a Google Drive folder with videos, mostly of his wife, Erika Kirk, that were uploaded on September 15, 2025, five days after Kirk’s assassination. (Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point spokesperson, told me that “I can pretty much guarantee we aren’t working with a Latvian company” and that none of the contractors the nonprofit works with are familiar with the clipping campaign.)

A separate Discord server, called US Politics Clipping, is run by a young Norwegian named Anders Wedøe, who runs ClipSon, a Norwegian clipping company. US Politics Clipping links to the same Google Drive as Elephant Clipping. The folder includes videos of figures including Shirley, President Trump, and Vice President Vance, as well as the ESPN sports commentator Stephen A. Smith. US Politics Clipping displays a monthly budget of $125,000, and its users are restricted to posting only clips edited from the videos provided in the Google Drive. Wedøe declined to speak about his business’s involvement in politics.

When I described Elephant Clipping to Whitney Phillips, a professor at the University of Oregon’s School of Journalism and Communication, she told me, “That’s just social media now.” Phillips was only half-joking. Short-form video clips have become ubiquitous. “This moment is so disorienting. When you’re looking right at something, you don’t have enough information to describe what you’re seeing,” Phillips said. In prior technological cycles, many ads, such as television commercials, were obvious. On social media, many are unlabeled, especially those in the form of short videos, and they sometimes aim to convey the impression of a groundswell that doesn’t exist.

The Discord server doesn’t specify who is paying Elephant Clipping or the other right-leaning political-clipping operations, but Google Drive folders in each of the Serviuos and Wedøe-run campaigns are filled with files uploaded by what appear to be three employees of Enclave & Key, a Las Vegas–based marketing company: Jules Katz, the chief of staff; Benjamin Goodman, a vice president of operations; and Jack O’Hara, the head of media production at an Enclave & Key subsidiary. O’Hara and Katz seem to have uploaded videos to the Google Drive with their company email address. In at least one instance, O’Hara also used what appears to be his personal email address. It’s not specified what role, if any, Enclave & Key plays in the campaigns.

Enclave & Key’s CEO and founder is Blake Wynn, the 26-year-old nephew of the billionaire and conservative mega-donor Steve Wynn. (ClipSon runs a clipping campaign for Steve Wynn with a $10,000 monthly budget, which directs participants to a Google Drive of videos seemingly uploaded by Goodman.) Enclave & Key’s services include connecting influencers to brands, organizing branding events, and other types of marketing, according to the company website.

When I reached out to Blake Wynn with a list of questions, he responded that “there are a number of inaccuracies” but declined to offer further clarification and didn’t follow through on an invitation to talk. Enclave & Key told me in an emailed statement that “news has been clipped and shared for generations” and described itself as an “American company engaged in a routine, longstanding and lawful practice, despite attempts to sensationalize it by invoking high-profile conservative names and portray it as something nefarious.” Steve Wynn didn’t respond to a request for comment. Shortly after I first reached out to both Wynns, Enclave & Key, and others involved in the campaigns, the deletions started.

By Thursday afternoon, video folders for clippers that had been uploaded to a Google Drive by Katz and O’Hara had disappeared, though the same files were then posted by Goodman, who used an email address not linked to Enclave & Key. The Discord channels for US Politics Clipping and Elephant Clipping were also delisted from the publicly visible campaigns in the ClipSon and ClipIt Discords. The campaigns were still visible on Monster Lab, but descriptions explaining the purpose of each campaign were gone. On Friday morning, Enclave & Key Google Drives for the campaigns were taken down as well.

Blake Wynn has connections beyond his uncle in the conservative mediasphere. During a November 2025 interview on the sports-focused podcast Bring the Juice, he said that he and Enclave & Key “do a lot of work in politics.” Wynn also said that he regularly speaks with FBI Director Kash Patel, and that he was good friends with Kirk. In the same podcast, Wynn recounted sitting next to Trump at Mar-a-Lago on Election Night in 2024, alongside Elon Musk, UFC CEO Dana White, and Steve Witkoff, Trump’s friend and special envoy. In the past several years, he’s posted pictures of himself on Instagram at small gatherings at the White House and at Mar-a-Lago, alongside the Kirks and Tulsi Gabbard, the former director of national intelligence.

Clipping campaigns may lack transparency, but they likely are legal. “There’s no clear-cut disclosure rules for these types of campaigns,” Saurav Ghosh, a campaign-finance expert at the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan, pro-democracy nonprofit, told me. “This seems like a clear case of why we need more transparency rules for digital content so badly.”

Elephant Clipping has some areas that are out of bounds, for reasons that aren’t made clear. Clippers are instructed not to post videos of the journalist Megyn Kelly, the commentators Nick Fuentes and Tucker Carlson, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., or the anti-trans activist Riley Gaines, among others. Banned subjects include the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol and the cryptocurrencies that members of the Trump family have promoted. In the Turning Point USA campaign, clippers are barred from posting videos of Candace Owens, who has become an Erika Kirk antagonist.

Clippers are also prohibited from telling people to “vote for” or “vote against” individual candidates or causes and cannot suggest that viewers “donate” specific causes. It’s possible, experts told me, that these limits are intended to avoid triggering campaign-finance regulations that would require the funder behind the campaign to be identified or to avoid content-moderation rules on social-media platforms. Two sub-campaigns in the Discord offer extra money for clippers to post favorable videos about Vivek Ramaswamy—a GOP candidate for Ohio governor—and Gabbard. Serviuos also manages clipping campaigns for the conservative influencers Ben Shapiro and Steven Crowder. Both campaigns are listed on Monster Lab with $30,000 budgets for last month, and Crowder’s campaign also links to an Enclave & Key–connected Google Drive. (Neither Shapiro nor Crowder responded to requests for comment.)

Blake Wynn claims to have met with both Ramaswamy and Gabbard. He said during his interview on Bring the Juice that he’d shared a car with Ramaswamy as a part of Trump’s 2024 Election Night victory motorcade. Last year, when Gabbard became director of national intelligence, Wynn posted pictures of himself with her at the swearing-in ceremony, along with a caption that read in part: “I don’t think this will be my last time in the Oval Office with YOU!” Gabbard resigned in June. (Ramaswamy and Gabbard didn’t respond to requests for comment.)

A decade after political interference on social media involving overseas actors first became a major issue, the pattern is repeating as the midterms approach. In 2018, Philip Howard, a researcher at the Oxford Internet Institute, called attempts to influence elections via social media “the new normal.” Elephant Clipping and its related campaigns show just how prescient he was.
